prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: B013 is the only shortlisted entry that eight of eight members ranked, and seven placed it in their top three, so the support is broad rather than dependent on one subfield. The scientific case is a clean one: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light-shift problem that limited neutral-atom clocks, and the strontium experiments, above all Ye's, took the systematic uncertainty to about 1e-18 and added many-body clock physics. It is a single, clearly defined invention with an unambiguous two-person credit, two decades of independent confirmation across Sr, Yb and other species in many national laboratories, and concrete consequences: tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the route to a redefinition of the second. It also follows naturally from the ion-trap prize of 2012 and the frequency-comb prize of 2005 without repeating either.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and overlap. Lattice clocks rest on frequency-comb and ultrastable-laser techniques already honoured in 2005, and on ion-clock work honoured in 2012, so a sceptic can ask whether this is a refinement of recognised work rather than a new discovery. Other groups (Takamoto, the Paris and German laboratories) contributed to the early demonstrations, and the relative weight of Katori's proposal versus Ye's performance advances is a judgement call. The redefinition of the second has also not happened yet, so the practical impact is still partly prospective.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the Higgs observation first but concedes that credit is spread over two collaborations of thousands, that any three-person choice among the four credited names is partly arbitrary, and that her pick rests on remembered roles.
responses.response: I agree with that diagnosis of the attribution problem, and it is the main reason I rank B001 below B013. The physics and the importance are not in doubt, but a prize that has to choose three of four founders, with Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee and Gianotti all defensible, will be contested however it is drawn. B013 has none of that difficulty. I do not think the contested credit makes the Higgs discovery less worthy, and I would support it if the committee finds a configuration it can defend, but I would not put it ahead of a clean invention.

responses.point: Danielsson places the Higgs discovery first as the central unrecognised experimental result of the era, observed independently by two detectors and confirmed through Run 1 to Run 3, and he treats the experiment-leader trio as fair but disputable.
responses.response: I accept that the Higgs discovery is the largest experimental result on the list and that the 2013 prize left it unrecognised. Where I differ is on whether leadership roles in a very large collaboration map onto the Nobel criterion of a discovery attributable to named individuals. His own trio omits Della Negra, and he says so. I would also point out that his second choice is the optical lattice clock with the same two names I propose, so our difference is one of ordering and of how much weight attribution deserves, not of substance.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first, as I do, citing the magic-wavelength concept, record systematic uncertainty and the route to redefining the second, but she flags overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and the contributions of other groups.
responses.response: I share her atomic-structure reading and agree that the overlap with 2005 and 2012 deserves a direct answer. My answer is that the lattice clock is a distinct enabling idea, since magic-wavelength trapping gives many atoms interrogated at once and so the stability that ion clocks cannot reach, rather than a refinement of combs. I also agree the Paris and German groups are real contributors, but I do not think that disturbs a two-person credit built on the proposal and the record-setting realization.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the Higgs first and IceCube second, and puts the lattice clock third, valuing instrumentation that opens a new observational window.
responses.response: I read his ordering as consistent with mine in kind: he values instrument-led discovery, and the lattice clock is exactly that, an instrument that opens relativistic geodesy and constant-variation searches. I would ask whether the astrophysical-neutrino result, which I do not rate highly enough to rank, can be attributed to three names as cleanly as he suggests. I leave that to the committee members closer to astroparticle physics.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes.
The relative weight of Katori's proposal and Ye's performance advances, and whether other early contributors should be considered outside the supplied credit.
Whether the redefinition of the second will have taken place by the time of the decision, which would strengthen the maturity argument.
Whether a Higgs configuration of three of four names could be defended well enough to outrank B013 in the majority view.
statement.conflict_note: Possible perceived connection, not a documented conflict: I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory during my doctoral period and Jun Ye is associated with Hall's group. I also work in atomic physics and quantum optics, in the same broad community as the candidates, and have Lund and WACQT quantum-technology ties. The committee may wish to consider whether recusal on B013 is advisable.
